title: The Buddha Tends the Sick Monk
text:
According to the monastic rules of early Buddhism, the Buddha was once walking through the lodgings of a monastery with his attendant Ananda when they found a monk lying sick with dysentery. He was too weak to get up and lay in his own filth. Nobody was looking after him.

The Buddha asked him why no one cared for him. The monk answered that he had been of no use to the other monks, so they did not attend to him.

The Buddha sent Ananda for water. Together they washed the man, the Buddha holding his head and Ananda his feet, and laid him on a bed.

Then the Buddha called the monks together and asked whether there was a sick monk in that place and why nobody tended him. They gave the same answer: he had done nothing for them. The Buddha reminded them that they had left their families and had no mother or father to care for them. If they did not look after one another, who would? And he told them that whoever wished to tend him should tend the sick. From then on, caring for a sick member became a duty of the community.
lesson: A community proves itself in how it treats members who cannot repay it. Looking after the weakest is not charity on the side, it is part of the work.
